transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-03-18 11:00 PT | Duration: 45m | Attendees: Sam (Redwood AE), Maya (Redwood SE), Liam (Redwood SE), Jared (Infra), Priya (ML), Nora (PM), Alex (Security)

[00:00] Sam: hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick agenda — sizing follow-up from last week, burst planning, and any security asks. we'll keep it tight.

[00:14] Jared: yeah thanks Sam. we got some internal feedback — main ask is how we avoid overspending during spikes. our traffic is pretty spiky around 10am and 3pm.

[00:25] Priya: and we saw the p95 latency bump during the demo run when a couple of heavy requests hit. trying to understand whether dedicated pools can smooth that without crazy cost.

[00:36] Maya: totally — so high level, Dedicated lets you reserve a pool (min nodes) and then we can configure autoscale up to max nodes with a burst buffer. important knobs: warm pool size, scale up/down cooldowns, and forced burst capacity which can be metered as overage.

[00:51] Nora: can you clarify burst buffer vs autoscale? seems similar.

[00:56] Liam: yeah quick, burst buffer is a short-term cushion — we pre-warm ephemeral containers or allow short-lived overage that bypasses full scale out. autoscale is slower but cheaper if sustained. think of burst for <2min spikes.

[01:12] Jared: ok so if we have a 30s spike of high token count requests, burst handles it, but if it continues past the cool-down it will spin up more nodes?

[01:20] Maya: exactly. the policy we proposed last week had min 2 nodes, max 12, burst buffer of 20% capacity, scale-up threshold at 80% CPU/KV cache hit miss ratio, and a 60s scale-up evaluation window. scale-down with 5m cool-down to avoid thrash.

[01:36] Priya: that 60s window — is that real-time or averaged? because we're sensitive to short-lived flurries.

[01:42] Maya: it's an averaged window across the metrics we monitor — token rate and KV miss rate. you can tune to shorter windows but that risks flapping. for your 30s spikes burst buffer is ideal.

[01:53] Alex: from security perspective — how are overage logs and audit events recorded? we need full traceability for any requests that get routed to burst vs dedicated pool.

[02:02] Sam: good call. we log routing decisions with request ids, auth principal, and model variant. logs are sent to your SIEM via S3 or syslog — we also have audit export for privileged actions.

[02:13] Alex: do you support customer-managed KMS for model cache encryption?

[02:18] Maya: yes, for Private we support customer KMS; for Dedicated we can integrate with your cloud KMS and encrypt local cache and attachments. will capture in security deep-dive.

[02:27] Priya: on model variants — is quantized model always cheaper? we saw some quality diffs last week.

[02:33] Liam: quantized models reduce memory and increase throughput, but yes can affect quality depending on prompt/temperature. our recommendation: run perf-quality sweep — Redwood Optimize can give suggested quantization profiles based on your eval set.

[02:46] Priya: can we do a quick example? our default workload is multi-turn chat with long context — 6k tokens typical.

[02:53] Maya: for long contexts, KV cache hit rate plays big role. if many prefixes repeat across users, cache reduces compute. but if every convo is unique, cache helps less and you need more baseline nodes.

[03:05] Jared: we attached some sample traffic yesterday. it's mostly unique, but there are repeated templates for summarization flows.

[03:12] Sam: got it. so two prongs: 1) we run sustained throughput benchmark to show how many tokens/sec a given Dedicated pool supports for your model variant; 2) you provide 7-day traffic so Maya can recommend autoscale thresholds and warm-pool sizes.

[03:28] Priya: how do you measure sustained vs burst — what's the metric?

[03:32] Maya: sustained is tokens/sec over 5–15 minute windows at p95 throughput. burst is peak tokens/sec over 30s windows. we give both numbers plus cost per 1M tokens for each.

[03:42] Nora: any examples of cost math? we want to show execs.

[03:45] Sam: we'll send a pricing sheet with scenarios — e.g., baseline 4-node pool for typical traffic, autoscale to 10 nodes for sustained surges, with burst buffer covering short spikes. we'll include per-token and per-node overage examples so you can see dollar impact.

[03:59] Jared: on cool-downs — 5m seems long. our spikes are short but frequent, like every 15m. won't 5m cause nodes to remain warm and raise cost?

[04:09] Maya: it's a balance — shorter cool-down reduces cost for short spikes but increases risk of oscillation and extra spin-ups. suggestion: set cool-down to 2m and add hysteresis on metrics (require sustained threshold for two evaluation windows). we can simulate with your traces.

[04:24] Priya: can Redwood simulate and give expected cost distribution?

[04:27] Liam: yes, if you give us observed arrival trace and p95 token sizes we can run a simulator and show expected node-hours and burst overage.

[04:36] Alex: audit + compliance — please confirm SOC 2 controls, retention window for logs, and where logs live regionally. we have EU residency requirements.

[04:45] Sam: we have SOC 2 in progress and can share the report once signed. logs can be stored in-region, and Dedicated in our EU region keeps data in-region; for Private you can control on-prem. we'll include a security doc link after call.

[04:58] Priya: any constraints on model switching? if we fallback to a cheaper variant during heavy load, how are hallucination/regression risks mitigated?

[05:06] Maya: Redwood supports canary rollouts and automatic fallback policies. you can set quality thresholds on eval prompts; if the cheaper variant fails threshold we fallback to primary. logs capture model variant and quality comparisons.

[05:18] Jared: great. so immediate asks to Redwood: run sustained 10k-token/sec benchmark and share logs; send pricing scenarios; simulate autoscale with our trace.

[05:27] Sam: yes — we'll take those. Maya to run benchmark; Sam to send pricing. schedule security deep-dive with Alex. any other blockers?

[05:36] Nora: timeline — we want decision by end of month to align procurement. can Redwood commit to deliverables in two weeks?

[05:43] Sam: yes, pricing by 3/20, simulation and benchmark by 3/25, security dive week of 3/23 — should fit.

[05:51] Priya: final — what's the experience if we exceed max nodes? will requests fail or get rerouted to hosted?

[05:58] Maya: by default requests will queue briefly and then return a 429 if capacity exhausted; but you can enable cross-region fallback to hosted API at your risk (data egress) or configure a graceful degraded variant.

[06:12] Jared: we prefer graceful degrade with a cheaper model rather than 429.

[06:16] Sam: noted, we'll include that in the config options.

[06:20] Alex: and please include audit of any fallback events.

[06:23] Sam: will do. recap and next steps — Sam share pricing, Maya run benchmark and upload logs, customer share traces, schedule security deep dive.

[06:35] Priya: thanks everyone.

[06:37] Sam: thanks, bye.
